76:22.ar: إِنَّ هَٰذَا كَانَ لَكُمۡ جَزَآءࣰ وَكَانَ سَعۡيُكُم مَّشۡكُورًا
76:22.en: (And it will be said unto them): Lo! this is a reward for you. Your endeavour (upon earth) hath found acceptance

76:23.ar: إِنَّا نَحۡنُ نَزَّلۡنَا عَلَيۡكَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَنزِيلࣰ ا
76:23.en: Lo! We, even We, have revealed unto thee the Qur'an, a revelation

76:24.ar: فَٱصۡبِرۡ لِحُكۡمِ رَبِّكَ وَلَا تُطِعۡ مِنۡهُمۡ ءَاثِمًا أَوۡ كَفُورࣰ ا
76:24.en: So submit patiently to thy Lord's command, and obey not of them any guilty one or disbeliever

76:25.ar: وَٱذۡكُرِ ٱسۡمَ رَبِّكَ بُكۡرَةࣰ وَأَصِيلࣰ ا
76:25.en: Remember the name of thy Lord at morn and evening

76:26.ar: وَمِنَ ٱلَّيۡلِ فَٱسۡجُدۡ لَهُۥ وَسَبِّحۡهُ لَيۡلࣰ ا طَوِيلًا
76:26.en: And worship Him (a portion) of the night. And glorify Him through the livelong night

76:27.ar: إِنَّ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ يُحِبُّونَ ٱلۡعَاجِلَةَ وَيَذَرُونَ وَرَآءَهُمۡ يَوۡمࣰ ا ثَقِيلࣰ ا
76:27.en: Lo! these love fleeting life, and put behind them (the remembrance of) a grievous day

76:28.ar: نَّحۡنُ خَلَقۡنَٰهُمۡ وَشَدَدۡنَآ أَسۡرَهُمۡۖ وَإِذَا شِئۡنَا بَدَّلۡنَآ أَمۡثَٰلَهُمۡ تَبۡدِيلًا
76:28.en: We, even We, created them, and strengthened their frame. And when We will, We can replace them, bringing others like them in their stead

76:29.ar: إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦ تَذۡكِرَةࣱۖ فَمَن شَآءَ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِۦ سَبِيلࣰ ا
76:29.en: Lo! this is an Admonishment, that whosoever will may choose a way unto his Lord

76:30.ar: وَمَا تَشَآءُونَ إِلَّآ أَن يَشَآءَ ٱللَّهُۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمࣰ ا
76:30.en: Yet ye will not, unless Allah willeth. Lo! Allah is Knower, Wise

76:31.ar: يُدۡخِلُ مَن يَشَآءُ فِي رَحۡمَتِهِۦۚ وَٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ أَعَدَّ لَهُمۡ عَذَابًا أَلِيمَۢا
76:31.en: He maketh whom He will to enter His mercy, and for evil-doers hath prepared a painful doom

76:5.ar: إِنَّ ٱلۡأَبۡرَارَ يَشۡرَبُونَ مِن كَأۡسࣲ كَانَ مِزَاجُهَا كَافُورًا
76:5.en: Lo! the righteous shall drink of a cup whereof the mixture is of Kafur

76:6.ar: عَيۡنࣰ ا يَشۡرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ ٱللَّهِ يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفۡجِيرࣰ ا
76:6.en: A spring wherefrom the slaves of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly

76:7.ar: يُوفُونَ بِٱلنَّذۡرِ وَيَخَافُونَ يَوۡمࣰ ا كَانَ شَرُّهُۥ مُسۡتَطِيرࣰ ا
76:7.en: (Because) they perform the vow and fear a day whereof the evil is wide-spreading

76:8.ar: وَيُطۡعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ مِسۡكِينࣰ ا وَيَتِيمࣰ ا وَأَسِيرًا
76:8.en: And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him

76:9.ar: إِنَّمَا نُطۡعِمُكُمۡ لِوَجۡهِ ٱللَّهِ لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمۡ جَزَآءࣰ وَلَا شُكُورًا
76:9.en: (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you

76:10.ar: إِنَّا نَخَافُ مِن رَّبِّنَا يَوۡمًا عَبُوسࣰ ا قَمۡطَرِيرࣰ ا
76:10.en: Lo! we fear from our Lord a day of frowning and of fate

76:11.ar: فَوَقَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلۡيَوۡمِ وَلَقَّىٰهُمۡ نَضۡرَةࣰ وَسُرُورࣰ ا
76:11.en: Therefor Allah hath warded off from them the evil of that day, and hath made them find brightness and joy

76:12.ar: وَجَزَىٰهُم بِمَا صَبَرُواْ جَنَّةࣰ وَحَرِيرࣰ ا
76:12.en: And hath awarded them for all that they endured, a Garden and silk attire

76:13.ar: مُّتَّكِـِٔينَ فِيهَا عَلَى ٱلۡأَرَآئِكِۖ لَا يَرَوۡنَ فِيهَا شَمۡسࣰ ا وَلَا زَمۡهَرِيرࣰ ا
76:13.en: Reclining therein upon couches, they will find there neither (heat of) a sun nor bitter cold

76:14.ar: وَدَانِيَةً عَلَيۡهِمۡ ظِلَٰلُهَا وَذُلِّلَتۡ قُطُوفُهَا تَذۡلِيلࣰ ا
76:14.en: The shade thereof is close upon them and the clustered fruits thereof bow down

76:15.ar: وَيُطَافُ عَلَيۡهِم بِـَٔانِيَةࣲ مِّن فِضَّةࣲ وَأَكۡوَابࣲ كَانَتۡ قَوَارِيرَا۠
76:15.en: Goblets of silver are brought round for them, and beakers (as) of glass

76:16.ar: قَوَارِيرَاْ مِن فِضَّةࣲ قَدَّرُوهَا تَقۡدِيرࣰ ا
76:16.en: (Bright as) glass but (made) of silver, which they (themselves) have measured to the measure (of their deeds)

76:17.ar: وَيُسۡقَوۡنَ فِيهَا كَأۡسࣰ ا كَانَ مِزَاجُهَا زَنجَبِيلًا
76:17.en: There are they watered with a cup whereof the mixture is of Zanjabil

76:18.ar: عَيۡنࣰ ا فِيهَا تُسَمَّىٰ سَلۡسَبِيلࣰ ا
76:18.en: (The water of) a spring therein, named Salsabil

76:19.ar: ۞وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وِلۡدَٰنࣱ مُّخَلَّدُونَ إِذَا رَأَيۡتَهُمۡ حَسِبۡتَهُمۡ لُؤۡلُؤࣰ ا مَّنثُورࣰ ا
76:19.en: There wait on them immortal youths, whom, when thou seest, thou wouldst take for scattered pearls

76:20.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَيۡتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيۡتَ نَعِيمࣰ ا وَمُلۡكࣰ ا كَبِيرًا
76:20.en: When thou seest, thou wilt see there bliss and high estate

76:21.ar: عَٰلِيَهُمۡ ثِيَابُ سُندُسٍ خُضۡرࣱ وَإِسۡتَبۡرَقࣱۖ وَحُلُّوٓاْ أَسَاوِرَ مِن فِضَّةࣲ وَسَقَىٰهُمۡ رَبُّهُمۡ شَرَابࣰ ا طَهُورًا
76:21.en: Their raiment will be fine green silk and gold embroidery. Bracelets of silver will they wear. Their Lord will slake their thirst with a pure drink

47:38.ar: هَٰٓأَنتُمۡ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ تُدۡعَوۡنَ لِتُنفِقُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَمِنكُم مَّن يَبۡخَلُۖ وَمَن يَبۡخَلۡ فَإِنَّمَا يَبۡخَلُ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦۚ وَٱللَّهُ ٱلۡغَنِيُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلۡفُقَرَآءُۚ وَإِن تَتَوَلَّوۡاْ يَسۡتَبۡدِلۡ قَوۡمًا غَيۡرَكُمۡ ثُمَّ لَا يَكُونُوٓاْ أَمۡثَٰلَكُم
47:38.en: Lo! ye are those who are called to spend in the way of Allah, yet among you there are some who hoard. And as for him who hoardeth, he hoardeth only from his soul. And Allah is the Rich, and ye are the poor. And if ye turn away He will exchange you for some other folk, and they will not be the likes of you

16:103.ar: وَلَقَدۡ نَعۡلَمُ أَنَّهُمۡ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّمَا يُعَلِّمُهُۥ بَشَرࣱۗ لِّسَانُ ٱلَّذِي يُلۡحِدُونَ إِلَيۡهِ أَعۡجَمِيࣱّ وَهَٰذَا لِسَانٌ عَرَبِيࣱّ مُّبِينٌ
16:103.en: And We know well that they say: Only a man teacheth him. The speech of him at whom they falsely hint is outlandish, and this is clear Arabic speech

blMtoHlTEnI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Insan, Part 4: Verses 22-31
blMtoHlTEnI.one_line: Closing Al-Insan: accept the whole Quran, five commands for reaching Paradise, the lovers of the fleeting, and a will that exists only by Allah's will.
blMtoHlTEnI.summary: Closing Al-Insan, he recaps the three elements every da'wah needs and why Allah tells the people of Paradise their effort earned it, so no one feels like an impostor. Verse 23 is loaded with emphasis: Allah alone sent the Quran down exactly as it should be, so every verse must be heard. There is no cherry-picking in Islam; a Muslim may fail to practise a verse but cannot deny it, or he follows earlier nations who kept a line or two of their books. Then come five commands for those who want Paradise: persevere until Allah's decree, as in the boycott years; do not follow the sinful or ungrateful; remember the name of your Lord through the working day, since we cannot imagine Allah but can attach our hearts to His name; prostrate at night; and glorify Him through long nights. The deniers love the immediate and leave a heavy Day behind them, like a student who takes the trip of a lifetime and fails the exam. Allah can replace any people, as faces come and go in the masjid. Whoever wills finds a path, but that will itself comes from Allah, so take no credit, keep making the intention and ask to be admitted into His mercy.

outline.heading: Opening
Why know the last four ajza: 64 surahs, one concept each
outline.gist: The aim is for the last four ajza to be understood in English and memorized. They hold 64 of the Quran's 114 surahs, and every surah, long or short, teaches one concept: Al-Baqarah as much as Al-Kawthar.

outline.heading: Reason, reward and warning: the three elements of da'wah
outline.gist: Da'wah must speak to the intellect and the deeper meaning of life, to the desire for reward, and to what a person risks. Drop one and people accept a message they misunderstood; each surah carries all three, and this passage puts its weight on reward.

outline.heading: Personal service in Paradise
outline.gist: Services lose their personal touch when they go global, so one might fear being one of billions in Paradise. Allah details who will serve you and how every desire is met, so nothing here, not even a private yacht and crew, outranks it.

outline.heading: A reward, and your effort is appreciated
outline.gist: No one could repay Allah, let alone earn Paradise, yet He tells its people again and again that they earned it. That spares them the guilt and impostor's doubt people feel at great blessings in this life.

outline.heading: Sent down by Allah alone, exactly as it should be
outline.gist: His final advice in the surah begins with the Quran itself. Following the verb with its own root (nazzalna ... tanzila) stresses the act was done perfectly, by Him alone and in the right sequence, so nothing in it is filler to skip.

outline.heading: No cherry-picking: Islam is not an open buffet
outline.gist: To reach Paradise you take, accept and try to practise the whole Quran. Where scholars differed there is latitude, but clear absolutes cannot be dropped because they are inconvenient, a habit more common today than ever.

outline.heading: Walking in the footsteps of earlier nations
outline.gist: The Prophet warned that Muslims would follow the nations before them step by step. Many followers of earlier faiths have not read their own book and keep one or two parts, treating the rest as suggestions; the Quran is accepted word by word, none of it hidden or embarrassing.

outline.heading: Failing to practise is not denying
outline.gist: A man with an alcohol problem who knows it is haram and sees himself at fault differs from one who calls the ruling outdated. All of us fall short in practice, but rejecting a single verse takes a person out of Islam.

outline.heading: Counting the emphases in one verse
outline.gist: Inna, the royal we, nazzalna and the repeated root all stress that Allah alone sent it, so we listen to every part. Emphasis signals importance in Arabic, and scholars count a verse's emphases and reflect on why there are so many.

outline.heading: First command: persevere until your Lord's decree
outline.gist: Perhaps revealed during the three-year boycott of Banu Hashim, the lowest point of the da'wah. The decree is left unnamed, relief or not; whoever wants Paradise holds on to patience and grit until it comes.

outline.heading: Second command: do not follow the sinful or ungrateful
outline.gist: Tuti' is more than obeying; it is walking in someone's footsteps. It recalls the surah's opening, where a guided human ends up either grateful or ungrateful.

outline.heading: Third command: remember the name of your Lord
outline.gist: The Quran distinguishes remembering Allah, your Lord and the name of your Lord. The name may mean all His names, or the name Allah: every other name can be extended in some measure to a creature, for good or ill, but no one can be Allah.

outline.heading: We cannot picture Allah, so we attach to His name
outline.gist: A relationship normally needs some image, as a description of the Prophet lets you picture him. Describing Allah is kufr, since He is exalted above face and organs, so the heart attaches to His name, which it can write and hold in mind.

outline.heading: Those who said too much about His essence
outline.gist: Disagreements in creed came from scholars who spoke about what cannot be articulated. The wise either stopped at what Allah said of Himself or interpreted the words to keep Him exalted; anything more led to error.

outline.heading: His name in every masjid and on every tongue
outline.gist: That is why His name hangs in every masjid: it is what we have. Morning and evening means always, going to work or coming back, with His name on the tongue at every action.

outline.heading: Lovers speak of the beloved
outline.gist: People in love talk of nothing else, to their friends' annoyance. Whoever loves Allah speaks of Him even alone, and whoever remembers Him in himself or in a gathering is remembered by Him in return.

outline.heading: Choose a name you love: ar-Rahman
outline.gist: A heart that wants to love but does not know how can hold on to the name Allah or a name it loves. Ar-Rahman was a coinage the Arabs had never heard, and it drew people so strongly that Quraysh claimed he learned from a man called Rahman.

outline.heading: Fourth command: prostrate to Him at night
outline.gist: After the working day, give part of the night to prostration, meaning prayer.

outline.heading: Fifth command: glorify Him through a long night
outline.gist: Tasbih declares Allah free of every flaw: He is not human, not at fault, and not to be objected to or held to account.

outline.heading: Two practical commands, three spiritual
outline.gist: Persevere through the hard years ahead and do not sell out; then keep His name on your tongue while working as farmer, physician or taxi driver, and give the night to prostration and glorification. These five lead to the reward just described.

outline.heading: They love the immediate and leave a heavy Day behind
outline.gist: The deniers want everything now, with no patience to plan for anything greater. They may enjoy the world in ways you never imagined, and it means nothing, because they have put a heavy Day behind a wall.

outline.heading: The trip before the exam
outline.gist: The epic trip that costs a failed exam and a lost year never makes up for it. Someone who shrugs that off cannot be trusted; no one would hire him or give him a daughter in marriage.

outline.heading: We created them, and We can replace them
outline.gist: Their strength is Allah's gift, used for everything wrong, and He can bring others just as strong who will not turn away, as the end of Surat Muhammad warns.

outline.heading: Replaced in the service of the masjid
outline.gist: Every year new faces come and others vanish for years, each with a good excuse of work, research or family. His only dua is to be kept in the service of Allah's house.

outline.heading: Whoever wills will find a path
outline.gist: The surah is a reminder: whoever truly wants it and makes the intention finds the path back to his Lord, and Allah eases the way.

outline.heading: You only will because Allah wills
outline.gist: The will in your heart exists only because Allah willed you to will. If even the will needs His permission, what of the doing?

outline.heading: His mercy as a place you enter
outline.gist: Yudkhilu man yasha'u fi rahmatihi makes mercy a place you are brought into rather than an abstract idea. All we do is ask Him to see us worthy of it.

outline.heading: The Friday Fajr custom in Syria
outline.gist: In Syria the imam recites As-Sajdah and Al-Insan at Friday Fajr, lowers his voice at this verse, and the whole congregation responds. As a child he found it strange; later he saw it answers the surah's question of how anyone reaches Paradise.

outline.heading: Ask from your weakness: the equation never adds up
outline.gist: Nothing you do can earn Paradise, and even your intentions and choices are His gift. Accept that you have little, turn to Him with that weakness and ask to be entered into His mercy; the oppressors face a painful punishment.

outline.heading: A second reading: He admits those who have the will
outline.gist: The verse can also mean He admits into His mercy those with the will described before. Either way, make the intention to find your way to Him, knowing it is His gift, and do not complicate what is simple.

outline.heading: Fall and ask again: a weekly appointment
outline.gist: Every time you fall or fail, say the same thing again. That is why Al-Insan is recited every Friday: one of the few surahs you have a weekly appointment with.

outline.heading: No full credit when He owns all of you
outline.gist: Separate creations can take full credit for their own work, but your spirit, choice and free will are His creation and He owns every part of you. The deen centres on niyyah because it is all you have, and even that is by His permission.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Dawah, outreach and representing Islam
themes.note: Honest da'wah addresses reason, reward and warning together; leaving one out leaves people with a misunderstood message.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Paradise gives each person individual care, and Allah tells its people they earned it so they feel no guilt at their bliss.

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran: reading, reflecting, living it
themes.note: Every verse was sent down deliberately; accept the entire Quran, admit failings in practice, but never deny or sideline a verse.

themes.label: Patience (sabr) and perseverance
themes.note: Persevere until Allah's decree comes, whatever it turns out to be, as the Prophet did in the boycott years.

themes.label: The Names and Attributes of Allah
themes.note: Since Allah cannot be imagined, the heart connects to His name; Allah is the one name no creature shares, and ar-Rahman was a new coinage.

themes.label: Love: of Allah, the Prophet, and one another
themes.note: Those who love speak constantly of the beloved; remember Allah and He remembers you.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: Night prostration and long glorification are the spiritual commands that lead to Paradise.

themes.label: Delayed gratification vs love of the immediate (al-'ajilah)
themes.note: The deniers trade a heavy Day for immediate pleasure; short-termism makes a person unreliable even by worldly standards.

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette
themes.note: Serving the masjid is an opportunity Allah can take away and give to others; ask Him to keep you in His house's service.

themes.label: Intention and sincerity (niyyah, ikhlas)
themes.note: Whoever wills finds a path, but the will is Allah's gift; niyyah is all you have, so keep renewing it and ask to be entered into His mercy.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: You cannot take credit for good deeds when your spirit, choice and free will are all Allah's creation.

69:25.ar: وَأَمَّا مَنۡ أُوتِيَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِشِمَالِهِۦ فَيَقُولُ يَٰلَيۡتَنِي لَمۡ أُوتَ كِتَٰبِيَهۡ
69:25.en: But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: Oh, would that I had not been given my book

m4UZ6-0mcrk.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Mortality, Episode 31
m4UZ6-0mcrk.one_line: Closing session on mortality: build the capacity to contemplate, accept Allah's right to judge, aim for the highest Jannah, and guard the sincerity of deeds.
m4UZ6-0mcrk.summary: He argues that reminders of death and judgment only work if a person can genuinely contemplate them, putting himself inside the scenes the Quran describes the way the companions did. That skill, once natural through idle daydreaming, has been eroded by constant scrolling, and he likens contemplation to a mock interview: preparation for something that will certainly happen, not fantasy. He then sets out conditions for accountability to shape a life: taking Allah's warnings seriously rather than exempting oneself, accepting deep down that Allah has every right to judge you even though the ego hates being judged, and being certain that resurrection is not too complex for the One who began creation. Without fear of divine accountability, he says, morality collapses into whatever is legal or undetected. The core message is ambition: since Allah has opened the doors of Jannah, aiming low is a lack of respect. For someone who aims high and works hard, the only real danger is deeds hollowed out by showing off, vanity or envy, as in the hadith of the reciter, scholar and martyr thrown into the fire first. He closes by framing judgment as accountability before the One who loves you most, warning against complacency, and promising that a life aimed at the hereafter brings its own joy.

outline.heading: Opening
Contemplation is the skill that makes mortality work
outline.gist: Simulate your own death regularly; the companions were moved by the Quran because they lived each scene as their own.

outline.heading: A lost capacity: daydreaming replaced by scrolling
outline.gist: People once sat and thought deeply for long stretches; today's flood of stimuli leaves no room to process, so the skill must be rebuilt.

outline.heading: Contemplation as a mock interview, not imagination
outline.gist: Like medical students rehearsing a real interview, picturing the Day of Judgment is preparation for a certain event so you can avoid the wrong outcome.

outline.heading: The scholar who lay in a mock grave
outline.gist: A great imam would lie between his bed and the wall, walk himself through death and questioning, then remind himself he was still alive and could change.

outline.heading: The companion struck down by a verse
outline.gist: One companion was so shaken by a verse that he stayed home and let people visit him as if sick, too embarrassed to say why.

outline.heading: Children live stories fully
outline.gist: His childhood reaction to a violent film shows how children feel what they hear; adults let this mirroring grow rusty.

outline.heading: Keeping the heart alive through lived reminders
outline.gist: The ability to feel a description does not vanish; it must be exercised so the Quran's reminders keep the heart awake.

outline.heading: Why reminders of the Day are scattered through every surah
outline.gist: Nearly every surah returns to judgment several times so that a fading heart is constantly revived.

outline.heading: Condition: take Allah's warnings seriously
outline.gist: Assuming it will not happen to you is exempting yourself without evidence.

outline.heading: Condition: accept that Allah has the right to judge you
outline.gist: The ego resents judgment, especially accurate judgment; you must accept deep down that Allah is worthy of judging you and that you deserve it.

outline.heading: Condition: certainty that resurrection is not too complex
outline.gist: Some accept God but balk at being remade; the One who began creation will repeat it and bring each person back individually.

outline.heading: Without accountability morality is a joke
outline.gist: Inner accountability before the All-Seeing is what restrains people when something is legal or undetectable.

outline.heading: How the Prophet united people of every background
outline.gist: Diverse people came to share one set of values because the Quran kept placing the Day of Judgment before them.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr vomits food bought with riba
outline.gist: He forced out food he learned was from usurious wealth though he was not obliged to, out of the scrupulousness the hereafter produced.

outline.heading: The questions to ask yourself
outline.gist: Do you take it seriously, believe it will happen to you, think it too complex, and accept Allah's right to hold you to account?

outline.heading: You choose which of the two groups you join
outline.gist: The Quran always presents two opposite outcomes; nothing forces you into one, your life now writes which it will be.

outline.heading: Embrace mortality instead of fleeing it
outline.gist: Living ready for death removes the fear and makes life better.

outline.heading: High ambition for Jannah
outline.gist: Low ambition when Allah offers the highest levels is poor etiquette; ask for al-Firdaws and live to qualify for it.

outline.heading: What can still go wrong: rejected deeds
outline.gist: For one who aims high, the risk lies in deeds rejected through faulty mechanics, which are easily learned, or corrupted intention.

outline.heading: The first three thrown into the fire
outline.gist: The reciter, the scholar and the martyr who acted for people's praise used Allah's name as a cover for seeking fame.

outline.heading: Ignorance is forgiven, ostentation is not
outline.gist: Honest mistakes are pardoned, but deliberate showing off, envy and arrogance turn mountains of deeds into weightless fluff.

outline.heading: Mortality and sincerity are internally connected
outline.gist: Taking death seriously drives you back to examine intention and ihsan in every deed.

outline.heading: The Prophet aimed for the highest station yet feared
outline.gist: He asked for al-Wasilah while fearing the fire; the companions, even those promised Jannah, guarded against one drop of heart disease poisoning their deeds.

outline.heading: A focused life with an achievable goal
outline.gist: Such people have no time for gossip and enjoy life because their goal is achievable and demands all their energy, including refining the quality of deeds.

outline.heading: Accountability before the One who loves you most
outline.gist: Judgment by the One who loves you more than your parents is of a different nature; a scholar preferred Allah's reckoning to his parents'.

outline.heading: Mercy is no excuse for neglect
outline.gist: Taking Allah's love as reason for carelessness ignores His clear warnings; balance hope with fear.

outline.heading: Meet me at the Basin
outline.gist: The Prophet told those inviting him to leisure that they would have all the time in the world once they reached the Hawd.

outline.heading: Aim high and the joy comes on its own
outline.gist: Chasing fun yields misery while aiming at the hereafter brings it naturally; living for the weekend wastes most of the week.

outline.heading: Outro

FdLkq6W99Dw.title: A Plan for Ramadan
FdLkq6W99Dw.one_line: A ten-point plan for Ramadan: intention, fasting with excellence, Quran, dhikr, prayer, knowledge, relationships, service, dua, and planning your life.
FdLkq6W99Dw.summary: Respecting an opportunity means planning for it, and Ramadan never arrives by surprise. After the hadith in which the Prophet describes Ramadan as a month of blessing in which Allah watches His servants compete and boasts of them to the angels, he lays out ten points to write down. First, set a clear and sincere intention, since people themselves judge deeds by their motives, and aim for this to be your best Ramadan ever. Second, fast with excellence: fasting is not a handicap but proof of how little you need, a step further from the forbidden, and a training of the self that should extend to the tongue, eyes, ears and hands. Third, enjoy the Quran through a daily portion that is never skipped and a few verses kept for reflection, since Ramadan is the annual Quran retreat. Fourth, build daily dhikr in place of irritation, chatter and scrolling. Fifth, invest in prayer, with the young standing the full taraweeh. Then commit to daily learning, repair broken relationships, serve others, learn dua as an art and write your duas down, and use the quiet of fasting to plan your life's direction, even though the plans themselves will change.

outline.heading: Opening
The companions anchored their year on Ramadan
outline.gist: They spent months asking to reach Ramadan and months asking for its acceptance; even people far from Allah find closeness when He opens the gates of Paradise.

outline.heading: Respecting an opportunity means planning for it
outline.gist: Ramadan never comes as a surprise, so plan well; he has already booked off the last ten nights of next year's Ramadan.

outline.heading: A month of barakah: the smallest deed amplified
outline.gist: In the hadith of the blessed month, barakah means Allah turning something small into something far greater, as He made everything from nothing.

outline.heading: Competing to lift each other and Allah boasting of His servants
outline.gist: Allah sends mercy, removes sins and accepts dua, then watches people compete to motivate one another and shows them off to the angels who doubted humanity; so show Him your best.

outline.heading: Point one: deeds are only as good as their intention
outline.gist: Even outside religion people feel betrayed when they learn a kind act had another motive, and marriages and friendships end over it; Allah too judges actions by what they aimed at.

outline.heading: Ask why you fast and pray; write your goals
outline.gist: Decide now what you want from the month, from closeness to Allah to changing habits or companions, so you can keep checking whether you have reached it.

outline.heading: Intend this to be your best Ramadan
outline.gist: Keep standing goals plus one specific to this year; the moment you look back on an earlier Ramadan as your best, you have started going backwards.

outline.heading: Point two: fasting is not a handicap
outline.gist: Treating the fast as an excuse to be tired, unproductive or irritable turns it into a handicap; it shows how little you need and removes the constant distraction of food.

outline.heading: One step further from haram; taming the self
outline.gist: Giving up the lawful puts you further from the forbidden, so scrolling or gossiping while fasting makes no sense; Allah has no need for the hunger of someone who keeps lying.

outline.heading: If you can skip the midday tea, you can do anything
outline.gist: Not making a cup of tea after his morning clinic proves to him that the self can be tamed from temper, gossip and arrogance too.

outline.heading: Fasting with every limb, in your own context
outline.gist: Withhold the tongue, eyes, ears, hands and feet from sin; for him excellence means giving patients full attention and being present with his children without complaining.

outline.heading: Point three: enjoy the Quran
outline.gist: Everything about the Quran is beautiful, artistic, intellectual and emotional, and it serves the simplest and most complex minds alike; it saved us before and will again.

outline.heading: A daily portion you never skip
outline.gist: The Prophet told those who missed their nightly portion to make it up in the morning; pick an amount you can keep, a juz or a page, and carry it beyond Ramadan.

outline.heading: Scholars who set hadith aside for the Quran
outline.gist: He was taught to do nothing in Ramadan but read Quran, as great hadith scholars, including Imam Malik, closed their classes for the month and devoted themselves to it.

outline.heading: Recite continuously and contemplate a few verses
outline.gist: He keeps reading without counting khatmas, while spending weeks on a few verses or a surah, reading and listening to what scholars say about them.

outline.heading: Ramadan's status comes from the Quran
outline.gist: The month is honoured because the Quran was revealed in it, so focusing on the Quran is focusing on its reason; Ramadan is our annual Quran retreat.

outline.heading: Point four: dhikr instead of venting or scrolling
outline.gist: When fasting makes you want to snap, turn to remembrance; there is no halal scrolling, only meaningless clips or worse.

outline.heading: Start small and build a daily wird
outline.gist: The Prophet taught a daily portion of Quran and dhikr; one of his teachers built over fifty years from a hundred to ten thousand salawat a day.

outline.heading: Simple numbers that add up
outline.gist: Three hundred on the way to work and back, a hundred after each prayer and before sleep quickly passes a thousand with little effort.

outline.heading: Dhikr instead of chatter before prayer
outline.gist: Sit in remembrance during the talk before Isha instead of chatting, so the heart calms; the Prophet's one thing to hold onto was a tongue moist with remembrance.

outline.heading: Point five: invest in your prayer
outline.gist: Around four hundred rakat of taraweeh in a month is practice for finding the heart in prayer, so that afterward prayer is rest rather than a burden.

outline.heading: Young people: never leave taraweeh early
outline.gist: He forbids young men from skipping or leaving taraweeh early while their knees work and they have time; those who leave do not sleep earlier anyway.

outline.heading: Standing beside the Ka'bah as a boy
outline.gist: His father worked at the Zamzam pumps and left him in the Haram, where he squeezed in by the rail and prayed the full taraweeh, his best memories to this day.

outline.heading: Pray every prayer in congregation, even at home
outline.gist: Do not miss a daily prayer, pray in congregation as often as possible, with a roommate or relative if not at the masjid, and listen to the whole Quran in prayer.

outline.heading: Point six: commit to a daily lesson
outline.gist: Ramadan is when scholars release their best series; find someone you connect with and learn something every day.

outline.heading: The mind works best on an empty stomach
outline.gist: Memorization doubled or tripled in Ramadan; as a child he memorized a whole juz in one day, page by page.

outline.heading: Point seven: revive severed relationships
outline.gist: Fix ties with parents, relatives and estranged friends at the start of the month for your own clean heart, and call someone you have neglected for years each day.

outline.heading: Point eight: be of service
outline.gist: With the right intention, volunteering earns the reward of the prayer you missed as well as the service; give, teach, or help however you can.

outline.heading: Teaching his brother Quran at fifteen
outline.gist: He taught his youngest brother and two cousins, finished with them in Ramadan with gifts and a celebration none of them forgot; teenagers should find a child to teach.

outline.heading: Badr was in Ramadan: a month of action
outline.gist: Many decisive events in Islamic history fell in Ramadan; it is not a month to sit at home but to serve.

outline.heading: Point nine: dua is an art
outline.gist: Speaking to the King of kings differs from speaking to any creature; in dua you lay out fears, hopes and the emotions you wish you had or did not have, with hands raised as the Prophet did.

outline.heading: Write down your duas for sujud
outline.gist: Write and memorize the duas you will make in every prostration of the month and keep building this conversation.

outline.heading: Point ten: worship by planning your life
outline.gist: Use the month to ask what you will do with your few laps around the sun and what your legacy will be; planning shows what you care about even if the plan fails.

outline.heading: What is your role in the victory you pray for?
outline.gist: When praying for the ummah's success, think about the steps it requires, your role in them, and make dua for your first step.

outline.heading: The notebooks he carried out of Syria
outline.gist: Fleeing at night, he packed his planning notebooks instead of clothes; none of his milestones happened, but planning gave him a direction toward Allah that held.

outline.heading: Recap of the ten-point plan
outline.gist: He runs back through all ten points, adding that being of service is the way out of selfishness and that dua answers the Quran in which Allah spoke first.

outline.heading: Outro

-qLENfQWGk8.title: Bounties of Ramadan
-qLENfQWGk8.one_line: The hadith of Salman on what Ramadan offers, then five bounties to pursue: forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, immense reward, Laylat al-Qadr and answered dua.
-qLENfQWGk8.summary: He wants people to enter Ramadan excited and focused on what it offers. From the Prophet's sermon at the end of Sha'ban he draws the month's features: obligations outweigh any voluntary act and are multiplied seventyfold, patience is rewarded without reckoning, hunger should turn attention to people who have no choice, provision grows through appreciation rather than income, and giving iftar shifts the focus from feeding yourself to feeding others. He regrets that Ramadan has become a night-time food festival. Then come the five bounties to memorize. Forgiveness of sins requires feeling their weight, fasting out of faith rather than social pressure, and sincere repentance so you are clean inside by Eid. Freedom from the Fire is granted every night to those who compete hardest; he describes Jahannam on the Day of Judgment to show what that freedom means and says the Generous never takes it back. Immense reward includes fasting's unnumbered reward and the priority of obligations, so Isha in congregation comes before taraweeh. Laylat al-Qadr, the night that made the month, teaches quality over quantity and is lost through grudges, so reconcile and seek it all ten nights. Finally, Allah answers dua directly, so prepare your duas.

outline.heading: Five things to carry into the month
outline.gist: Focusing on five bounties brings the most benefit and excitement for Ramadan.

outline.heading: Salman's hadith: a great and blessed month
outline.gist: His teachers narrated it despite questions about its chain; the Prophet told the companions of a month of blessing with a night better than a thousand months, an obligatory fast and recommended night prayer.

outline.heading: Obligations outweigh voluntary acts, multiplied seventyfold
outline.gist: Any voluntary deed in Ramadan equals an obligation outside it and each obligation equals seventy, given how far obligations outrank extras.

outline.heading: Month of perseverance: reward without reckoning
outline.gist: The patient walk straight to the front on Judgment Day; the anxiety before Ramadan usually fades after the first days, but some resilience is still needed.

outline.heading: Month of consolation: feel for those with no choice
outline.gist: Afternoon hunger reminds you that many live this way without choosing it; Ramadan is only 8.3 percent of your year, so turn from comforting yourself to comforting others.

outline.heading: Provision grows through appreciation
outline.gist: The paycheck does not change but appreciation does, which is why the first workday after Ramadan feels easy, and the same balance can panic one person and delight another.

outline.heading: We turned Ramadan into a festival of food
outline.gist: Eating copious amounts at night for thirty days is unhealthy and not the Prophet's way; Ramadan means less food, less sleep and fewer distractions.

outline.heading: Feeding the fasting shifts the focus
outline.gist: Giving iftar earns forgiveness and freedom with the faster's full reward, turning the natural urge to eat into a search for someone else to feed.

outline.heading: Feeding those who fast from poverty
outline.gist: The reward also covers those hungry because they have nothing; poor workers in the Haram earning almost nothing still walked around every night offering their dates.

outline.heading: Even a sip of water; drinking from the Prophet's basin
outline.gist: Those too poor to host can give a sip of water or milk; whoever fills a fasting person will drink from the Prophet's basin and never thirst again. The month moves through mercy, forgiveness and release.

outline.heading: Bounty one: Jibril's dua against the unforgiven
outline.gist: Forgiveness of all sins is guaranteed to those who follow the month's teaching; Jibril prayed against anyone who lives through Ramadan unforgiven and the Prophet said amin.

outline.heading: Feel the weight of your sins
outline.gist: The bounty means little unless sin troubles you; the believer feels it as a mountain about to fall, the hypocrite as a fly brushed off his nose.

outline.heading: Fasting out of faith, not social pressure
outline.gist: Faith and seeking reward mean fasting because Allah commanded it; try at some point to fast where no one else is fasting.

outline.heading: His father reminded of Ramadan by a man named Ramadan
outline.gist: Isolated in Toronto without a masjid, his father had forgotten Ramadan was coming until an Egyptian guest named Ramadan asked about suhoor.

outline.heading: Night prayer and the last ten: easier routes to forgiveness
outline.gist: When fasting the whole month properly seemed hard, the Prophet added praying the nights and standing on Laylat al-Qadr, so at least commit to the last ten and start over with a clean slate.

outline.heading: Ramadan to Ramadan, and sincere repentance
outline.gist: Ramadan to Ramadan wipes out sins as long as major sins are avoided, but make deliberate tawbah from repeated sins so you are clean inside, not just in new clothes, on Eid.

outline.heading: Bounty two: shackles broken
outline.gist: Everyone is chained to punishment by ongoing sins; the word for freedom is the freeing of a slave, so that when Jahannam moves the freed are not dragged with it.

outline.heading: Freed every night: a competition, not a lottery
outline.gist: Allah frees people every night and more in the last ten, but only the top few who show their best; that night will matter more than any graduation, wedding or award.

outline.heading: Jahannam brought forth with seventy thousand reins
outline.gist: Each rein is held by seventy thousand angels, and every nation will fall to its knees at the sight.

outline.heading: When his knees buckled before a hyena
outline.gist: As a sixth-grader carrying groceries he saw a hyena on his uncle's well and lost the feeling in his legs; real fear makes even the bravest collapse.

outline.heading: Glancing at Jahannam from the corner of the eye
outline.gist: People kneel with heads down in humiliation, daring only a sideways glance at the Fire.

outline.heading: One dip erases a lifetime of luxury
outline.gist: The person who lived in the greatest ease is dipped into the Fire once and swears he never knew any joy.

outline.heading: Freed for life: the Generous does not re-shackle
outline.gist: The freed person is far away in the shade of the Throne; it does not mean never sinning, but always returning, because Allah never takes back a freedom He grants.

outline.heading: Nothing in life is worth more
outline.gist: With that guarantee he would hand over his turban and go home to his children; without it no one is off the hook until the bridge is crossed.

outline.heading: Make the dua for freedom every night
outline.gist: Ask from the first night, not only the last ten: You commanded us to free slaves, so free us, Your servants.

outline.heading: Bounty three: the reward with no number
outline.gist: On the board of deeds every act has a number except fasting, which Allah rewards personally because no one could force you to do it.

outline.heading: Obligations above all voluntary prayer
outline.gist: All the taraweeh ever prayed will not equal one obligatory prayer; voluntary acts increase Allah's love but obligations come first.

outline.heading: A day broken without excuse loses its reward forever
outline.gist: One make-up day settles the debt, but that day's prepared reward can never be regained.

outline.heading: Isha in congregation before taraweeh
outline.gist: The centre's sweaters say Isha is better than taraweeh; choose it every time, while knowing that in Ramadan each taraweeh rakah equals an obligation outside it.

outline.heading: The man who lived one more Ramadan
outline.gist: A man who died a year after a martyred companion was seen higher in Paradise because he lived another Ramadan with its prayers and prostrations, which is why we ask for long life.

outline.heading: Bounty four: the night made the month
outline.gist: Ramadan is honoured because of the night the Quran was first sent down; we fast and pray the whole month to honour that memory.

outline.heading: Don't rush taraweeh: listen to the Quran
outline.gist: Avoid the quick eight; stand, or sit if your knees hurt, and listen, because this month celebrates the Book of Allah.

outline.heading: Better than a lifetime: quality over quantity
outline.gist: A thousand months is over 83 years, and the night is better still; the surah was revealed in Mecca before Ramadan existed, teaching that one night can outweigh a lifetime, as many great figures died young.

outline.heading: Seek it in all of the last ten nights
outline.gist: Growing up in Syria he cherishes the 27th, as Ibn Abbas held, but the stronger view is that it moves within the last ten, and counting from the end of the month flips odd and even.

outline.heading: Forgotten because two men quarrelled
outline.gist: The Prophet came out to tell them the night but forgot it while settling a quarrel, a sign that grudges ruin it; reconcile with parents, relatives and friends before the last ten.

outline.heading: Pardon beyond forgiveness
outline.gist: The Prophet's dua asks Allah, who loves to pardon, to pardon you, deleting even the sins you dread explaining; commit to all ten nights rather than showing up on the 27th.

outline.heading: Bounty five: 'I am near'
outline.gist: In the dua verse among the fasting verses Allah drops the word 'say' and answers directly; the fasting person's dua at iftar is not rejected.

outline.heading: Prepare and memorize your duas
outline.gist: Acceptance does not always mean getting what you want when you want it; prepare a list before Ramadan, repeat it in every sujud, and keep the line open after the month.

outline.heading: Ramadan has come: gates opened, devils chained
outline.gist: The Prophet told of a blessed month with Paradise opened, Hell closed, devils restrained and a night better than a thousand months; whoever misses its good is truly deprived.

outline.heading: Something changes when Ramadan arrives
outline.gist: Allah envelops people in the month with what they neglect all year; he can do in Ramadan what would exhaust him on any other day.

outline.heading: When the gates of Paradise open
outline.gist: If a door opening on your mother's cooking changes your day, imagine the effect of Paradise's gates open for thirty days.

outline.heading: Allah boasts of His servants to the doubting angels
outline.gist: The angels feared humans would spread corruption and bloodshed, but Allah knew about Ramadan's last ten nights; the deprived one is denied His mercy in it.

outline.heading: Recap of the five bounties
outline.gist: Forgiveness of sins, freedom from punishment, immense reward, the night of status and answered dua.

-edJa89BbQ8.title: Bounties of Ramadan (Arabic)
-edJa89BbQ8.one_line: Arabic lesson on the hadith of Salman and the five treasures of Ramadan: forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, immense reward, Laylat al-Qadr and answered dua.
-edJa89BbQ8.summary: A spiritual rather than legal lesson on what Ramadan holds. The month's rank comes from the Quran revealed in it. Working through the hadith of Salman, he presents patience as the other face of gratitude: when fasting takes away the blessings you thank Allah for, beautiful patience replaces complaint. Consolation grows from chosen hunger, which should remind the comfortable of the forced hunger of others, from patients in the Damascus hospitals where he worked to the starving in Gaza and Sudan. Provision increases in meaning as appreciation grows, so never belittle a blessing, a warning he aims especially at young people comparing themselves to peers. Giving iftar turns the hungry person's focus to feeding others, and Ramadan should mean less food and more nourishment for the soul. He then gives five treasures: forgiveness, which you must want and which requires fasting out of faith rather than social pressure, plus repentance from major sins; freedom from the Fire, earned by effort and never revoked; immense reward, where fasting's reward is kept by Allah and obligations outrank all voluntary acts; Laylat al-Qadr, sought across all ten nights with hearts cleared of grudges; and answered dua. He closes by urging people to book leave and give time to worship, as the Prophet did in i'tikaf.

outline.heading: Opening
The month's rank comes from the Quran
outline.gist: Ramadan became master of months and Laylat al-Qadr master of nights because the Quran was revealed in it; tonight's lesson is spiritual, not legal.

Salman's hadith: the sermon at the end of Sha'ban
outline.gist: Its chain is questioned, but every meaning has authentic support, as his teachers' teacher Sh. Abdullah Siraj al-Din said; the Prophet rarely gathered people outside Jumuah, which shows the weight of this address.

outline.heading: Patience as the other face of gratitude
outline.gist: Normally you owe Allah thanks for food, safety and health; fasting withholds them, so the alternative to gratitude must be beautiful patience rather than ingratitude or objection, rewarded without reckoning.

outline.heading: Month of consolation: the hospitals of Damascus
outline.gist: He worked in a hospital named al-Muwasat and in a cancer hospital where the fridge had no chemotherapy and he could offer only saline and painkillers; Ramadan is for comforting one another.

outline.heading: Chosen hunger and forced hunger
outline.gist: The comfortable forget the poor; hunger by choice should make you refuse to accept anyone being hungry by force while your own table at Maghrib is full.

outline.heading: Provision increases in meaning, not amount
outline.gist: In thirty years of fasting he never got a raise in Ramadan; the same balance angers one man and delights another, and hunger makes what you have look plentiful.

outline.heading: Never belittle a blessing
outline.gist: Belittling Allah's blessings is among the worst sins and a cause of losing them; look at those below you, not above.

outline.heading: Young people comparing themselves to peers
outline.gist: A boy who sees classmates with expensive headphones, branded sneakers and phones starts despising what his parents give him; be grateful for what you have.

outline.heading: Gaza and Sudan dying of hunger
outline.gist: People who look and are named like us, in Gaza and in Sudan, are literally starving to death; he prays for their relief.

outline.heading: Giving iftar turns your focus to others
outline.gist: Feeding a fasting person brings forgiveness, freedom from the Fire and his reward; the Prophet redirects the hungry person from feeding himself to feeding someone else.

outline.heading: The poor cleaners in the Haram with their dates
outline.gist: As a boy he saw gaunt workers earning a few hundred riyals walking around at Maghrib with dates and laban, seeking someone to feed for the reward.

outline.heading: A month to feed the soul
outline.gist: Ramadan is for less food, drink and sleep so you devote yourself to worship; the body is fed for eleven months, so give the soul at least half of one.

outline.heading: Even a sip of water; drinking from the Prophet's basin
outline.gist: For poor companions the reward comes even with a sip of milk, a date or water; whoever fills a fasting person drinks from the Prophet's basin and never thirsts again.

outline.heading: Treasure one: forgiveness, if you want the gift
outline.gist: A promise only delights someone who wants what is promised, so a Muslim must first feel how much he needs his sins forgiven.

outline.heading: The mountain and the fly
outline.gist: Ibn Mas'ud: the believer sees his sin as a mountain about to fall on him, the hypocrite as a fly on his nose.

outline.heading: Fasting alone after leaving Syria
outline.gist: Brothers who fled to Europe in the war found fasting alone lonely and hard; he told them it was the best fast of their lives, because faith means fasting for Allah, not for the crowd.

outline.heading: Fasting, night prayer and Laylat al-Qadr with faith
outline.gist: When fasting perfectly seemed too hard the Prophet added praying the nights and then standing on Laylat al-Qadr, so at least the last ten nights.

outline.heading: Jibril's dua on the minbar
outline.gist: Jibril prayed against the one who lives through Ramadan unforgiven and the Prophet said amin; what did he do to miss a month made for forgiveness?

outline.heading: Ramadan to Ramadan; repent of major sins
outline.gist: Each Ramadan wipes the slate except for major sins, so make tawbah from them; there is no point going to Eid clean outside and ruined inside.

outline.heading: Treasure two: freedom from the Fire by effort
outline.gist: Allah frees people every night and more in the last ten, but not by luck: He watches who competes hardest in good.

outline.heading: The best night of your life
outline.gist: Not graduation, wedding or a new job, but the night Allah declares you freed, never to see or hear the Fire.

outline.heading: Jahannam brought forth with reins
outline.gist: Jahannam is brought with reins each held by seventy thousand angels lest it devour the gathering, and every nation falls to its knees.

outline.heading: Knees buckling before a hyena
outline.gist: In sixth grade he froze at a hyena on a well in his village; on that day people kneel in humiliation and only glance at the Fire from the corner of their eyes.

outline.heading: Ask for freedom every night
outline.gist: Pray: You commanded us to free slaves, and we are Your slaves, so free us; and offer yourself through reading, prayer and effort.

outline.heading: Freed does not mean sinless; the Generous does not revoke
outline.gist: The freed person may sin but repents and returns quickly; once the Generous frees someone He never takes it back.

outline.heading: Treasure three: the reward with no number
outline.gist: On the board of deeds fasting has no number because Allah rewards it Himself, since only He can command you to leave what you work all your life to obtain.

outline.heading: Fasting is a private worship
outline.gist: No one can verify your fast, as adults tested children by checking their tongues; when you truly fast in secret Allah magnifies it.

outline.heading: Obligations versus voluntary acts
outline.gist: All the sunnah prayers of a lifetime together do not equal one obligatory prayer.

outline.heading: A day broken without excuse is lost forever
outline.gist: One day of make-up clears the debt but not the lost reward; Allah loves obligations most, and Ramadan multiplies them seventyfold.

outline.heading: Treasure four: the night of the Quran
outline.gist: Laylat al-Qadr made Ramadan great, and its value comes from the revelation, so the month is for absorbing and loving the Quran.

outline.heading: Stand and listen in taraweeh while you are young
outline.gist: Stand behind the imam holding the mushaf; if you do not stand while young, when will you? He hopes to lead two completions once the youth grow a bit.

outline.heading: A night better than a lifetime
outline.gist: A thousand months is a full lifetime, and the night is better, reminding us that lives are measured by good deeds, not length.

outline.heading: Quality over quantity: companions who died young
outline.gist: Mus'ab and others died in their twenties yet their names are blessed forever; on that night each prostration weighs like 83 years.

outline.heading: Seek it in all ten nights
outline.gist: He loves the 27th from his Syrian upbringing, but as Ibn Hajar notes it moves; the Prophet forgot it while reconciling two men and told them to seek it in the last ten, where odd and even depend on counting direction.

outline.heading: The night of pardon: clear your accounts
outline.gist: The Prophet taught Aisha to ask the Pardoning One for pardon, and Umar would declare people free of any claim against him before the last ten so he entered them clean.

outline.heading: Jibril returns each year to check on the Quran
outline.gist: Umm Ayman wept after the Prophet's death because Jibril no longer visited, yet he descends every Laylat al-Qadr with the angels and checks how the Quran is kept and followed.

outline.heading: Treasure five: the dua that is not rejected
outline.gist: The fasting person's dua at iftar is answered in one of several ways; train yourself in Ramadan to speak to Allah with your worries, hopes and repentance.

outline.heading: 'I am near': Allah answers without 'say'
outline.gist: In the verse among the fasting verses Allah drops the expected 'say' and speaks directly, tying Ramadan to answered dua.

outline.heading: The companions prepared their duas
outline.gist: They wrote and memorized duas for Ramadan and repeated them in every prostration until all were answered.

outline.heading: Ramadan has come: gates opened, devils chained
outline.gist: In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, Paradise opens, Hell closes, devils are chained, and whoever is denied Laylat al-Qadr is truly deprived, so make no excuses.

outline.heading: Book your leave for worship
outline.gist: He has already booked off Ramadan 2027; take leave to worship, not only to travel and eat.

outline.heading: I'tikaf is time set aside for Allah
outline.gist: I'tikaf has become something for the unemployed, but the Prophet deliberately set time apart in a small enclosure to be alone with his Lord.

outline.heading: The Prophet's night prayer in i'tikaf
outline.gist: Companions heard him pray and lined up behind the screen until the masjid filled; he stopped coming out so taraweeh would not become obligatory. He himself takes mornings off so he does not harm patients when exhausted.

outline.heading: Allah boasts of His servants to the angels
outline.gist: Allah envelops people with mercy in this month, watches them compete and boasts of them to the angels; the wretched is the one deprived of His mercy.

outline.heading: Outro

jliJgA4Fffc.title: The Fiqh of Ramadan
jliJgA4Fffc.one_line: A practical refresher on Ramadan rulings: intention, what breaks the fast and what does not, disputed cases, valid excuses, expiation, sunnahs, zakat al-fitr and Eid.
jliJgA4Fffc.summary: Treating it as a refresher of the questions people ask most, he walks through the rulings of Ramadan and his own choices among scholarly opinions, inviting people to follow the local imam if they wish. Obligatory fasts need an intention before dawn, and he adopts Imam Malik's view that one intention covers the month. One rule organizes the rest: whatever is taken in intentionally and nourishes the body, or its equivalent, breaks the fast. He lists six things that break it (intentional eating and drinking, intercourse or its equivalent, induced vomiting, intravenous nourishment, smoking, and menstrual or postpartum bleeding) and six that do not (brushing teeth, forgetful eating, wet dreams, non-nourishing injections, saliva and leftover wudu water). Of four disputed cases he holds that inhalers and drops do not break the fast while IV medication and suppositories do. Illness, travel, pregnancy or breastfeeding and severe fatigue are valid excuses, yet one should still intend to fast each night and break only when needed. He explains major and minor expiation and who owes each, the sunnahs of suhoor, early iftar and dua, taraweeh, zakat al-fitr and Eid, then answers questions on sports, swearing, zakat timing, paying zakat al-fitr in money and performance-enhancing drugs.

outline.heading: Opening
Intention the night before for obligatory fasts
outline.gist: Voluntary fasts can be intended in the morning, but Ramadan and make-up days need an intention before dawn; waking for suhoor already counts, and only forgetting it is Ramadan altogether fails.

outline.heading: One intention for the month and following the local imam
outline.gist: Imam Malik holds that one intention at the start covers the month, which he adopts; people may follow their madhhab or simply the opinions of the local imam they pray with.

outline.heading: The rule: intentional nourishment breaks the fast
outline.gist: Anything taken intentionally that provides nourishment in the medical sense, or its equivalent, invalidates the fast; most rulings follow from this.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, one: eating and drinking on purpose
outline.gist: Intentional eating or drinking ends the fast.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, two: intercourse or its equivalent
outline.gist: Full intercourse, or intentional ejaculation such as masturbation, breaks the fast; other intimacy does not but is risky.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, three: induced vomiting
outline.gist: Making yourself vomit on purpose breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, four: intravenous nourishment
outline.gist: Saline or IV nutrition, as given to patients who cannot swallow, nourishes the body and breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, five: smoking
outline.gist: Tobacco, cannabis or shisha break the fast without scholarly dispute, and breaking the fast on a cigarette is a poor way to thank Allah.

outline.heading: Breaks the fast, six: menstruation and postpartum bleeding
outline.gist: A woman in her period or postpartum bleeding cannot fast, without any sin on her.

outline.heading: Breaking the fast without excuse: a day lost for good
outline.gist: Doing any of the first five without excuse means a sinful broken fast that must be made up, and its reward never returns even if one fasted forever.

outline.heading: Does not break, one: brushing teeth and miswak
outline.gist: Brushing teeth is fine as long as nothing is swallowed; most scholars allow miswak all day.

outline.heading: Does not break, two: eating or drinking forgetfully
outline.gist: Allah fed and watered the forgetful person; do not remind someone mid-bite, but if you remember while chewing you must spit it out.

outline.heading: Does not break, three: a wet dream
outline.gist: Discharge in sleep, even in a daytime nap, does not affect the fast; only a ghusl for prayer is needed, but do not blur sleep and intent.

outline.heading: Does not break, four: non-nourishing injections
outline.gist: Intramuscular or subcutaneous antibiotics, blood thinners or insulin do not nourish and do not break the fast.

outline.heading: Does not break, five: swallowing saliva
outline.gist: Swallowing your own saliva is fine, even if gathering it first is distasteful.

outline.heading: Does not break, six: leftover water after wudu
outline.gist: Make wudu normally with rinsing; residual water is fine and needs no repeated spitting.

outline.heading: Disputed, one: inhalers
outline.gist: Scholars are divided; his view is that asthma or COPD inhalers do not break the fast, since they are neither nourishment nor recreation, but daily users should read up and decide.

outline.heading: Disputed, two: ear and eye drops
outline.gist: In his view they do not break the fast unless an anatomical opening lets them reach the throat or stomach.

outline.heading: Disputed, three: non-nourishing IV medication
outline.gist: He holds that even an IV antibiotic adds fluid to the vascular bed and so breaks the fast; anyone ill enough for an IV should probably break it anyway.

outline.heading: Blood tests versus donating blood
outline.gist: A blood sample does not break the fast, but donating half a litre or more does.

outline.heading: Disputed, four: suppositories
outline.gist: He holds they break the fast because they affect hydration, while acknowledging that choosing the other opinion is legitimate.

outline.heading: Valid excuse one: illness
outline.gist: Illness is a valid reason to break the fast, judged by the person; make up the days after Ramadan.

outline.heading: Valid excuse two: travel, and those always on the road
outline.gist: Travel permits breaking the fast, but those who commute long distances daily or drive for a living should usually fast, since they may never make the days up.

outline.heading: Travel then and now; a valid excuse keeps the reward
outline.gist: Travel in the Prophet's time was gruelling; today anything beyond about 82 km or outside the city counts, and a day broken for a valid excuse keeps its reward when made up.

outline.heading: Valid excuse three: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: Pregnant and breastfeeding women may break the fast.

outline.heading: Valid excuse four: severe fatigue
outline.gist: A roofer in July may break the fast when he risks harm, but must intend and begin fasting every day rather than skipping the month.

outline.heading: Long summer fasts in Canada and Germany
outline.gist: Arriving in July 2013 he found the long days harder than in Syria and Jordan, and workers in Germany fasting 21 hours could break the fast daily out of fatigue and make up later.

outline.heading: Never intend not to fast a day of Ramadan
outline.gist: With a passing illness or uncertain travel, intend to fast and decide in the morning; only the chronically ill skip the intention.

outline.heading: Make up missed days before the next Ramadan
outline.gist: Spread make-up days over the year instead of cramming them into the last week; delaying past the next Ramadan carries a penalty.

outline.heading: Major expiation: sixty days or feeding sixty
outline.gist: Freeing a slave no longer applies, leaving sixty consecutive days of fasting or feeding sixty people, roughly 1,200 dollars.

outline.heading: Intercourse is what triggers major expiation
outline.gist: Both consenting spouses owe it, paid by the husband; a wife pressured into it loses the day but owes no expiation.

outline.heading: Eating, drinking and masturbation: no major expiation in his view
outline.gist: Scholars differ on eating and drinking; he holds expiation applies only to intercourse, which is why people advise not marrying right before Ramadan.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: feeding one person per day
outline.gist: Fidya is one meal for a poor person for each day missed, at least 15 to 20 dollars today.

outline.heading: Fidya group one: the chronically ill
outline.gist: Those whose doctors say fasting will harm them, such as advanced kidney disease or familial Mediterranean fever, must not fast and pay fidya instead.

outline.heading: Those who cannot fast still honour the day
outline.gist: Menstruating, postpartum or ill people take only what they need privately during the day and eat their meal with the family at iftar, not a big midday meal out.

outline.heading: Medication every few hours; paying fidya ahead
outline.gist: Needing medication at set intervals counts as chronic illness; some pay the whole month's fidya in advance, though only days actually missed are owed.

outline.heading: Fidya group two: the elderly
outline.gist: There is no fixed age; the frail elderly do not fast and pay fidya for each day without ever making it up.

outline.heading: Fidya group three: postponed make-up days
outline.gist: Missing the deadline means one fidya per day, paid once, while the days are still owed; people with years of missed fasts should seek a fatwa from a scholarly body.

outline.heading: Fidya group four: pregnancy
outline.gist: A pregnant woman advised by her doctor not to fast breaks it; the husband pays the fidya and she still makes up the days.

outline.heading: Fidya group five: breastfeeding
outline.gist: The same applies to breastfeeding; unlike the ill and elderly, these last three groups still owe the days.

outline.heading: Sunnah one: suhoor, even a few dates
outline.gist: His father fried dates and bananas at suhoor; even if you have no appetite, take dates, water or fruit, since suhoor distinguishes our fast from that of the People of the Book.

outline.heading: Sunnah two: hasten the iftar
outline.gist: Break the fast immediately, on fresh dates, then dry dates, then water if you dislike dates.

outline.heading: Sunnah three: dua at iftar
outline.gist: The fasting person has a dua at breaking the fast, before or after.

outline.heading: Fasting from sin: a condition of acceptance, not validity
outline.gist: Lying or looking at the forbidden does not break the fast but removes its reward and acceptance.

outline.heading: Taraweeh: time in prayer matters, not the count
outline.gist: Eight or twenty rakat makes no difference; what matters is the time spent and the Quran recited.

outline.heading: Taraweeh at home or in the masjid
outline.gist: Both are valid; the masjid is better especially for children's sense of community, though some of his best Ramadans were praying at home with family and neighbours.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr: amount and who owes it
outline.gist: Fifteen to twenty dollars per family member, including a fetus past 120 days, owed by anyone with food for the day beyond their needs.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr: when to give it
outline.gist: It must go out before the Eid prayer; it is valid from the start of Ramadan, but the last ten days are best so families can buy food and clothes for Eid.

outline.heading: Eid prayer: strongly recommended, may be delayed
outline.gist: Treat it as a strongly recommended prayer; Eid al-Fitr may be delayed a little so people can still pay zakat al-fitr.

outline.heading: Eid prayer: whole families in open land
outline.gist: Men, women, children and even animals went out to an open field for Eid.

outline.heading: One Eid prayer for a community
outline.gist: Ideally a city gathers in one Eid prayer to unite, an ideal long lost today.

outline.heading: Q: sports and swimming are at your own risk
outline.gist: Recreational activity is allowed, but if it leads you to swallow water or break the fast from fatigue you are accountable.

outline.heading: Q: professional athletes
outline.gist: Most scholars do not treat sport as a livelihood, but he does: an athlete who takes precautions and is forced to break the fast has a valid excuse.

outline.heading: No one has to stop working to fast
outline.gist: A halal livelihood never has to stop for Ramadan even if it causes fatigue every day; make up the days later.

outline.heading: Q: swearing affects reward, not validity
outline.gist: Like holding wudu while daydreaming in prayer, swearing or conflict leaves the fast valid but strips its reward; validity is mechanics, acceptance is deeper.

outline.heading: Q: annual zakat is separate; pay it at the start of Ramadan
outline.gist: Regular zakat follows the lunar year, so fixing it at the start of Ramadan avoids miscounting days; zakat al-fitr is a separate Eid-morning duty.

outline.heading: Q: fidya for a chronically ill child
outline.gist: A parent who supports an adult child pays the fidya, optionally as a loan; such young people should learn to keep the appearance of fasting rather than treat Ramadan as not for them.

outline.heading: Q: paying zakat al-fitr in money
outline.gist: Hanafi scholars allow money and later scholars of other schools accept it; in Canada charities turn the money into food, so money is the practical choice.

outline.heading: Q: expiation is valued where you live
outline.gist: Fidya is priced by a meal in the city where you broke the fast, not by the cheapest country you can send it to.

outline.heading: Q: performance-enhancing drugs
outline.gist: They go beyond nourishment and break the fast; he warns young men that many advertised physiques are biologically impossible and come with liver and kidney damage.

outline.heading: Outro

-hQ3VyHeqxQ.title: Ramadan Preparation: Focusing on One's Self
-hQ3VyHeqxQ.one_line: Before Ramadan 1447: be a little selfish, sit honestly with yourself, run from the fire and live clean for thirty days.
-hQ3VyHeqxQ.summary: A khutbah given six days before Ramadan 1447, built on one instruction: this year, focus on yourself. He opens with 6:158 (faith will not help the soul that waits for the decisive signs) and 16:111 (every soul will come arguing for itself alone), and says the community's battery is empty after a hard year. Ramadan is the chance to sit in a session of self-honesty and ask where you are and whether you have drifted. Citing 66:6, he says Allah placed the fire where you can see it so you would run from it, and placed His love in the escape route: make escaping punishment your only goal and Jannah and love follow as consequences. As a father he would stand in for his children on that Day but cannot, and intercession comes later, so be a little selfish. His practical advice is to live clean for thirty days: strip social media and music from the phone, read Quran or reflect when you reach for it, fix your sleep. Hunger while fasting is a reminder that the spirit is hungrier still and needs its Lord. The second khutbah recounts the Prophet's first public sermon, in which he told even Fatima he could not save her from the fire, and the hadith qudsi on Allah loving the servant who keeps drawing near.

outline.heading: Opening
What are they waiting for? (6:158)
outline.gist: Are they waiting for the decisive signs of their Lord? When those signs come, faith will not benefit a soul that had not established it earlier or earned good through it. Do not wait.

outline.heading: Focus on yourself: every soul argues for itself
outline.gist: The battery is empty and we are running on fumes, so this Ramadan take for yourself what you need. Every person is held hostage by what they did; on that Day each soul comes to argue for itself alone and receives only the results of its own deeds.

outline.heading: A session of self-honesty
outline.gist: Sit with yourself honestly and ask: what do I seek, what do I need, where am I, where should I be going, am I still on track or have I drifted for a long time? Then 66:6: protect yourselves and your families from a fire fuelled by people and stones.

outline.heading: The fire in view, His love in the escape route
outline.gist: Allah placed the fire where you can see it so you would fear it and run the other way, and placed His love along your escape route. Ask to be freed from the chains that pull towards the fire, and you will find His love waiting.

outline.heading: Only one goal this year: escape punishment
outline.gist: Focus on not being punished; Jannah and loving Allah are natural consequences. On that Day you have nothing to argue with but your own choices, so focus on yourself, the only one you are responsible for.

outline.heading: No one can stand in for you: be a little selfish
outline.gist: As a father he wants to stand up and answer for his children, and for his parents, but cannot; intercession comes later, after each is held to account alone. So be a little selfish this year and make changes: live clean.

outline.heading: Live clean for thirty days
outline.gist: Strip social media from your phone, stop scrolling, and when you feel the urge to touch it, read Quran or reflect on a meaning you have not thought about in a while. Replace music with knowledge or a reciter you enjoy, and replace late nights with a better sleep schedule.

outline.heading: The hunger of the spirit
outline.gist: Try it for thirty days and you will feel different. A few hours without food or coffee and our temper frays with the children; the spirit's nourishment is its Lord, and it has been deprived far longer. Allah makes the body hungry to remind you the spirit is hungrier: give it one month out of twelve.

outline.heading: Ramadan is a miracle worker
outline.gist: Whatever you have done, Ramadan can put you back on track, changing you from the inside out. Less phone and scrolling, more sitting with your hands raised speaking to Allah.

outline.heading: A dua for yourself and the ummah
outline.gist: He models it: what you need, fear, lost and hope for, then the ummah, the children, the poor and the weak with no one to speak for them, starving and oppressed while you have more than you need. More of that this year, and you will find what you are looking for.

outline.heading: Make the full intention now
outline.gist: He does not know whether he will reach this Ramadan, let alone the next, so make a powerful intention now to use the month fully; if your days run out, you enter the grave with that intention and its reward.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Prophet's first public sermon
outline.gist: Commanded to warn his family at the start of his prophethood (26:214), he gathered them in the first sermon we have on record, and began by praising, magnifying and exalting Allah.

outline.heading: Save yourselves; I cannot do it for you
outline.gist: One responsible for others does not lie to them, and he warned of a severe punishment. To each tribe he said: save yourselves from the fire, for I cannot. He would have done it for them, but he could only teach them how to save themselves; they had to choose.

outline.heading: Fatima: all my wealth, but not the fire
outline.gist: O Fatima, daughter of Muhammad, ask me for whatever you want of my wealth, but I cannot save you from the fire. Make that the plan this Ramadan: sit with ourselves and save ourselves.

outline.heading: Draw near until He loves you
outline.gist: Pray every night to save yourself and you reach the hadith qudsi: My servant keeps drawing near to Me with extra worship until I love him; then he sees, hears and walks through Me, and if he asks I give him and if he seeks refuge I grant it.

outline.heading: Outro
